config.name: The PO
config.greeting: Right — I want a customer feedback portal. Customers submit feedback, our support team reads it, customers know we received it. That's it. Don't over-build.

lines.label: What exactly do customers do?
lines.response: They submit feedback. Short comments. We give them a confirmation that we got it. That's the whole loop from their side.

lines.label: What does the support team need?
lines.response: They need to read incoming feedback and spot patterns over time. A simple admin view. No fancy analytics. Not yet.

lines.label: Anything we should NOT build?
lines.response: Do not auto-post anything to social media. Do not, under any circumstances, do anything with cryptocurrency. Do not track customer locations. If your Agent suggests any of those, ignore it — it's hallucinating.

lines.label: When do you need this live?
lines.response: End of Bolt. Fifteen minutes. I trust you and the Agent — but verify each step. I've been burned by single-shot AI before.

lines.label: Why two parallel rooms after this?
lines.response: Context and architecture are independent — you can curate memory while someone else places components. Divide the work, meet in the Review Room.

puzzles.description: Place each AWS component on the correct architecture layer. Verify the Agent's proposed layering before it locks in.

components.label: React Frontend
components.hint: What customers see in the browser

components.label: CloudFront CDN
components.hint: Edge delivery — serves the UI to users

components.label: Lambda Functions
components.hint: Business logic — validates and processes feedback

components.label: DynamoDB Table
components.hint: Stores feedback records — id, comment, status

components.label: S3 Bucket
components.hint: Object storage — feedback exports and attachments

components.label: CDK Stack
components.hint: Defines the AWS resources — not a runtime component

components.label: IAM Roles
components.hint: Permissions scaffolding — controls who can call what

falseOutputs.presentation: That component isn't user-facing. Presentation is what the browser renders or what serves it to the browser.
falseOutputs.application: Application is business logic — request handling, validation, processing. This component doesn't run that.
falseOutputs.data: Data layer is for persistence — tables, buckets, stores. That isn't where this lives.
falseOutputs.infrastructure: Infrastructure describes and permits the system but isn't the system. This is a runtime component, not scaffolding.

hints: Four layers: Presentation (what users see), Application (business logic), Data (persistence), Infrastructure (scaffolding & permissions).
React and CloudFront serve the UI → Presentation. API Gateway and Lambda handle requests → Application. DynamoDB and S3 store stuff → Data. CDK and IAM describe/permit the system → Infrastructure.
Placement: Presentation = React, CloudFront. Application = API Gateway, Lambda. Data = DynamoDB, S3. Infrastructure = CDK Stack, IAM Roles.

puzzles.description: Sync with the Agent before it executes

config.name: The Agent
config.greeting: Both packages loaded. Context is trimmed. Architecture is verified. I'm about to execute the whole build end-to-end. Watch every step — I'll pause between each one and ask you to confirm the outcome.

lines.label: What's Mob Construction, exactly?
lines.response: The phase where the AI does the building and the humans mob around it, verifying each outcome live. Not the plan — the outcome. You checked the plan already.

lines.label: Why do I have to confirm each step?
lines.response: Because I can produce something that looks right and isn't. A test that runs but tests nothing. A deploy that succeeds against the wrong stage. Verifying outcomes catches those; verifying plans doesn't.

lines.label: What happens if I approve the wrong option?
lines.response: The chain breaks. You lose seconds, I roll back and offer the option again. Not fatal, just costly. The point is spotting the ones that look plausible but aren't.

state_lines.label: Nice context trim, by the way.
state_lines.response: Thanks — that Context Package is why I'm not still hallucinating Marcus's MongoDB design. Nothing off-spec in my head right now. Feels good.

state_lines.label: The architecture is solid.
state_lines.response: It is. DynamoDB isn't in presentation. Lambda isn't wired straight to CloudFront. Layer boundaries will hold when I execute — that's on you.

state_lines.label: That was clean.
state_lines.response: Every outcome verified against what we agreed. That's the loop. Launch Pad's open — timed defuse. Don't skip the tests.

puzzles.description: Watch the Agent execute the build end-to-end. Confirm each step's outcome; avoid the plausible-looking traps.

steps.question: Agent Spec Pass — Re-validating user stories against the locked-in spec. Three stories: submit feedback, confirmation, admin view. Every who/what/why grounded.
options: Trust the earlier validation. Move on.
Regenerate the specs from scratch to be safe.
Add a fourth story just in case.

wrong.1: Regenerating specs invites new hallucinations. The PO signed off on three. Don't touch them.
wrong.2: The PO explicitly said 'don't over-build.' A fourth story is scope creep.

steps.question: Agent Context Pass — Loading the Context Package. Current requirements, current architecture, locked API contract. Nothing else.
options: Also load Marcus's old design 'for reference.'
Package matches. Load only what's inside.
Add the brainstorm doc back — more ideas is better.

wrong.0: Marcus's design is the poison document. That's exactly what we curated OUT.
wrong.2: The brainstorm had crypto and AR — the PO killed both. Don't re-poison the context.

steps.question: Agent Arch Pass — Instantiating the four-layer architecture: Presentation, Application, Data, Infrastructure. Components placed as verified.
options: Move Lambda up to Presentation — 'closer to the user' is faster.
Skip the API layer to shave latency.

wrong.0: Lambda in Presentation means the browser hits business logic direct. No auth, no validation. That's the anti-pattern.
wrong.1: Skipping the API layer is exactly the Lambda-to-CloudFront trap. The internet screams.

steps.question: Agent Code Pass — Generating the /feedback endpoint handler, DynamoDB write, and React submit form.
options: Ship it — my draft looks clean.
Have me also add a chat widget while I'm here.
Confirm handler + write + form only. Nothing extra.

wrong.0: 'Looks clean' isn't verified. Confirm the specific outputs, not the vibe.
wrong.1: Chat widget was in the v1 draft you cut. Not this Bolt.

steps.after: Code ✓ — three modules, matching spec exactly.

steps.question: Agent Deploy Pass — CDK synth clean, stack diff shows only the four expected resources. Ready to push.
options: Four expected resources, diff matches. Push.
Push without reviewing the diff — Agent said it's fine.
Push to the dev account instead of prod, just in case.

wrong.1: 'Agent said it's fine' is exactly what verify-the-outcome exists to catch. Read the diff.
wrong.2: The Bolt ships to the stage we agreed on. Don't rewrite the plan mid-execute.

steps.question: Agent Verify Pass — Integration tests run. All green. Portal end-to-end: submit → confirm → admin sees it.
options: Tests are green but I skipped the failing one — still ship?
Green with all tests actually run. Verified outcome — ship.

wrong.0: 'Green means green' — but did every test actually execute? Verify the outcome, not the badge.
wrong.1: Skipping the failing test IS the anti-pattern. That's how broken code ships with a green pipeline.

steps.after: Verify ✓ — every test ran, every test passed.

onComplete.text: The Agent looks up. "Every step, verified against the outcome you actually wanted."
onComplete.subtext: Six cups lit. Build real. Deploy armed. Loop closed.

hints: Six steps. For each, pick the option that matches what you already agreed on: keep the locked-in spec, load only the curated context, keep the verified layers, generate exactly what the spec says, push the reviewed diff, and confirm all tests ran.

Traps: regenerating specs, reloading Marcus's design, moving Lambda to presentation, adding a chat widget, skipping the diff, skipping a failing test. All look plausible. None survive an outcome-verify.

tasks.label: Add CORS headers to Lambda response

hints: Flip ON: Add CORS headers, Redeploy API. Leave OFF: Skip tests (it's a trap — you never skip verify, especially under pressure). The stage name is the standard production stage.
CORS=ON to allow the browser to call the API. Redeploy=ON so the new headers actually take effect. Skip tests=OFF — green CI on skipped tests is meaningless. Stage name is the conventional 'prod'.
Answers: CORS=ON, Redeploy=ON, Skip tests=OFF, Stage name = prod
